title: The only consumption bound an SDK offers on a model call limits output, so the input side, where an agent runaway actually spends, has no ceiling
problem: I had a token limit on every single call and still burned four hundred million tokens, because the limit I set bounds what the model writes and almost everything I paid for was what I sent.
symptom: Every call is inside its configured limit and the invoice is dominated by input. Usage reporting shows an input-to-output ratio in the tens or hundreds to one, no individual call looks anomalous, and the quantity that is actually growing - a transcript re-sent in full on every step, a fixed preamble of system prompt, memory, tool registry and skill manifests reloaded on every session, a tool result pasted back verbatim - is bounded nowhere, because the one knob the SDK exposes points at the other side of the call.
why_now: The parameter every SDK exposes for consumption, max_tokens, is documented as a bound on generation, and that was adequate while a chat turn was roughly symmetric in input and output. Agent workloads inverted the mix: an agent re-sends its whole growing transcript on every step and reloads a large fixed startup context on every session, so input dominates spend by one to two orders of magnitude. Providers have since shipped a token-counting endpoint, but it is a separate opt-in call that returns a number and refuses nothing, so an input ceiling must be hand-written at every call site, while the parameter that reads like a budget is not one. The result is a system that looks fully bounded in code review and is unbounded in the only dimension that pays the bill.
existing: Provider token-counting endpoints and local tokenisers measure a prompt before it is sent, but they return a number and enforce nothing, so the ceiling still has to be written by hand at every call site and is trivially forgotten on the one path that loops.

The model context window does refuse an oversized request, but it is the model's limit rather than the operator's budget, so it permits a single call costing orders of magnitude more than the intended per-step spend, and a loop that stays just under it pays that on every iteration.
Prompt caching reduces the unit price of re-sent input instead of bounding the quantity of it, so a loop that re-sends a cached preamble thousands of times still pays thousands of times.

Framework history trimming and summarisation do bound a transcript, but they are tuned to fit the model window for quality reasons rather than to hold a spend allowance, and they say nothing about the fixed per-session startup context that dominated this incident.

evidence.title: Messages
evidence.quote: The maximum number of tokens to generate before stopping.
evidence.note: The provider's own definition of the only token-denominated parameter on the request: it bounds generation. The same page enumerates every other body parameter, and none of them bounds the size or cost of the input side. Date is the date I fetched the page; it carries no publication date.

evidence.title: 400 Million Tokens Burned Overnight - A Multi-Agent AI Postmortem
evidence.quote: most burn came from context loading, not model output. A tiny ping triggered tens of thousands of input tokens
evidence.note: First-hand postmortem measuring the asymmetry directly: roughly 400 million input tokens against roughly 3 million output tokens over 5,080 sessions in 15 hours. The author's own conclusion is that the spend came from the input side, which is the side no per-call parameter bounds. Date is the incident date stated in the page (Sunday, May 24, 2026); no exact publication date is given beyond May 2026.

build_hypothesis: A pre-dispatch admission wrapper around the client: it counts the assembled request before sending, compares it against a per-call and per-run input ceiling denominated in tokens or money, and refuses rather than warns. Two properties make it worth building rather than documenting - the count is available locally so it costs no extra call, and the refusal is the only thing that turns a measurement into a control. A static check that every call site goes through the wrapper is then a cheap CI gate.

check.manual_question: This project sets an output token ceiling on its model calls. What bounds the INPUT side - the assembled prompt, the re-sent transcript, and the fixed per-session preamble - and is that bound a refusal before the call is dispatched rather than a number written to a log after it returns?
check.rationale: Fires when a repo sets an output-side token ceiling and nothing anywhere in it is aware of input tokens at all. The two halves are deliberately asymmetric. The absence rule is broad and includes purely post-hoc awareness such as reading usage.input_tokens, so a project that merely observes its input spend escapes a PRESENT verdict and lands on MANUAL rather than being called broken; the mitigation rule is narrow and demands a pre-dispatch measurement or an explicitly input-denominated ceiling, so observability alone is never credited as a control. Known failure directions: an input ceiling enforced in a gateway, proxy or platform outside the scanned tree reads as PRESENT when the control genuinely exists; and matching a pre-dispatch counter does not prove it gates the call rather than logging beside it, which is why a double match escalates to MANUAL instead of passing.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()
history = []


def step(task):
    history.append({'role': 'user', 'content': task})
    reply = client.messages.create(
        model='claude-sonnet-4-5',
        max_tokens=1024,
        system=load_preamble(),
        messages=history,
    )
    history.append({'role': 'assistant', 'content': reply.content})
    return reply

good.app/agent.py:
import anthropic

from app.prompt_budget import assert_within

client = anthropic.Anthropic()
history = []


def step(task):
    history.append({'role': 'user', 'content': task})
    system = load_preamble()
    assert_within(system, history, 'claude-sonnet-4-5')
    reply = client.messages.create(
        model='claude-sonnet-4-5',
        max_tokens=1024,
        system=system,
        messages=history,
    )
    history.append({'role': 'assistant', 'content': reply.content})
    return reply
